title: The Writing on the Wall
summary: At a great banquet King Belshazzar drinks from the vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple and praises idols, and a human hand appears and writes on the palace wall. No wise man can read it until the queen recalls Daniel, who rebukes the king for his pride and interprets the words: his kingdom is numbered, weighed, and divided. That night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.
story: Decades have passed since chapter 4, and Daniel is now an old man, apparently forgotten at court. The vessels from the temple, carried to Babylon in 1:2, return to the story as the center of the offense. Chapter 4 showed a king humbled and restored; this chapter shows a king who knew that story and learned nothing (verse 22), and there is no restoration. Babylon, the head of gold, now falls, as the dream of chapter 2 foretold, and the next kingdom arrives. It is the first transfer of empire in the book, a small fulfillment that assures readers the rest will come too.
historical:
Belshazzar was the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon (556 to 539 BC). For many years he was known only from Daniel, and some scholars doubted he had existed. Babylonian texts discovered in the nineteenth century, including the Nabonidus Chronicle and other documents, confirmed him and showed that he governed Babylon for about ten years while his father lived at the oasis of Tema in Arabia. Though Babylonian records do not give him the formal title of king, he exercised royal authority. That explains a detail in the story: Belshazzar can offer only the position of third ruler in the kingdom (verse 7), because he himself was second.

The city fell to the Persian army of Cyrus in October 539 BC. The Babylonian record says it was taken without a battle. The Greek historians Herodotus and Xenophon later reported that the city fell while its people were celebrating a festival, which fits the scene of this chapter. Belshazzar is called Nebuchadnezzar's son, and Nebuchadnezzar his father. Nabonidus was not of Nebuchadnezzar's family, but in ancient usage father and son could mean ancestor and descendant or predecessor and successor; some have suggested a family link through Belshazzar's mother, though that cannot be confirmed.
cultural:
Royal banquets were displays of power, and ancient sources describe feasts on an enormous scale. Drinking from vessels captured from a defeated people's temple was a way of celebrating the victory of one's own gods over theirs. For Belshazzar to use the vessels of the LORD's house while praising gods "of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone" (verse 4) was deliberate mockery, and verse 23 names it as exalting himself against the Lord of heaven.

The queen who enters (verse 10) is probably the queen mother, since the king's wives are already at the feast. Queen mothers held real influence in ancient courts, and she remembers what the king has forgotten. The writing itself is a riddle. MENE, TEKEL, and PERES are Aramaic names for weights used in trade and in money: the mina, the shekel (a sixtieth of a mina), and the half-mina. Read as nouns, the words are a list of weights, which is why the wise men could perhaps read but could not understand them. Daniel reads them as verbs: numbered, weighed, divided. PERES also sounds like the word for Persia, and the kingdom is given to the Medes and Persians.
literary: The chapter mirrors chapter 4 and is built to contrast with it. Both kings are confronted by a supernatural message that the wise men cannot interpret, and both are addressed by Daniel. But where Daniel spoke gently to Nebuchadnezzar and urged repentance, he speaks sharply to Belshazzar, refuses his gifts (verse 17), and recounts Nebuchadnezzar's humbling as a lesson Belshazzar ignored. The scene moves from noise and revelry to silence and terror: the king's face turns pale and his knees knock together. The story ends abruptly, in two short verses, with his death, and the brevity is part of the judgment. In the Aramaic text, verse 31 is numbered as 6:1.

outline.t: Belshazzar's feast and the temple vessels
The hand writes on the wall
Daniel's rebuke: you knew and did not humble yourself
Belshazzar slain and the kingdom transferred

doctrines.note: Belshazzar is weighed and found deficient. God's judgment in this chapter is swift and final, and it falls not on ignorance but on a king who knew better (verse 22).

The feast praises gods of metal, wood, and stone that cannot see or hear or understand, while ignoring the God who holds the king's very breath (verse 23). Idolatry here is not only worshiping false gods but failing to glorify the true one.
The vessels set apart for God's house are treated as party cups. The chapter shows that what belongs to God cannot be profaned without consequence, even in exile when his temple lies in ruins.

words.note: Mene, the mina, a unit of weight and value. Daniel reads it as the verb to number: God has numbered the days of the reign and ended it. It is repeated, perhaps for emphasis, as if to say that the counting is complete.

Teqel, the shekel, a smaller weight. Daniel connects it with the verb teqal, to weigh: the king has been weighed on the scales and found deficient. The image of divine scales was familiar in the ancient world and appears elsewhere in Scripture (Job 31:6).

Peres, a half, probably a half-mina. Daniel reads it as divided, and the word also plays on paras, Persia. The inscription in verse 25 has the plural form, parsin, and the interpretation uses the singular. The wordplay makes the verdict and its executors a single word.

christ: The chapter's main contribution to the larger story is its witness that Babylon, the power that destroyed Jerusalem, fell exactly as God said. Isaiah and Jeremiah had foretold its fall, and Revelation takes up Babylon as the name for every proud world-power set against God: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great" (Revelation 18:2). Belshazzar's feast also resembles the rich fool in Jesus' parable, who planned to eat, drink, and be merry and was told, "This very night your life will be required of you" (Luke 12:20). Both teach that life and power are held from God. The good news, which Belshazzar never heard or heeded, is that the God who weighs the proud also gives grace, and in Christ he has come to bear the judgment his people could not survive. That is the gospel's answer to the writing on the wall.

hard.q: Why is Belshazzar called Nebuchadnezzar's son when his father was Nabonidus?
hard.a: In Semitic usage the words father and son had a wider range than in English. They could refer to an ancestor and descendant, or to a predecessor and successor on a throne: Assyrian records, for example, call the Israelite king Jehu the son of Omri, though he had overthrown Omri's dynasty. Those who read Daniel as sixth-century history hold that Belshazzar is called Nebuchadnezzar's son in this sense, perhaps with a family connection as well. Many critical scholars see the relationship as a simplification by a later author who knew Nebuchadnezzar as the great king of Babylon and Belshazzar as its last ruler. Either way, the chapter's point is the link between them: Belshazzar sat on the throne of a king whose humbling he had seen, and he chose not to learn from it.

questions: Belshazzar knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar and did not humble himself. What lessons have you seen others learn the hard way that you are tempted to ignore?
The feast treated holy things as trophies and toys. Where does our culture, or your own life, treat sacred things casually?
Daniel refused the king's gifts but still told him the truth. What does it look like to speak honestly to someone powerful without seeking their favor?
